notes:
These are verse-by-verse notes on Luke 11:1–27. One limit before you use them: I didn't find anything from the Lutheran sites (lcms.org, 1517.org), the Orthodox site (oca.org), or the modern-scholarship sites (netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org) for this passage. I also found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on these verses. So those views are left out, and the "different traditions" points below come only from the sources I did read. Several notes come from full pages I read; they have the URL only and no citation tag.

**v. 1**
- Guzik: the disciples waited until Jesus had finished praying, and what made them ask was watching how He prayed. He also notes that John the Baptist seems to have taught his own disciples about prayer. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-11/
- Constable: this is the fifth time Luke mentions Jesus praying. It's the only time in the Gospels that anyone asks Jesus to teach them something. Other Jewish groups, John's disciples among them, had their own prayers. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/luke-11.html
- Precept Austin: the disciple asked "teach us to pray," not "teach us a prayer" or "how to pray." The page also quotes Barclay: rabbis commonly gave their disciples a simple prayer to use regularly. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-11-commentary

**v. 2**
- Guzik: Jesus gave this prayer twice and worded it differently, which shows it wasn't meant as a fixed ritual or magic formula. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-11/ (Note: his commentary prints the longer NKJV wording, not the shorter BSB text.)
- **Disagreement among evangelicals:** Constable thinks Luke's introduction ("When you pray, say") suggests Jesus meant the words to be repeated as they are. In Matthew, he says, it's given as a model. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/luke-11.html Precept Austin, quoting Brian Bill, argues the opposite: the two different wordings show it wasn't meant to be memorised and recited. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-11-commentary
- "Father": Constable says the word is both close and respectful, and disciples can use it because of their relationship with Jesus. Guzik quotes D.A. Carson, who found no evidence of anyone before Jesus addressing God this way. On "hallowed": Constable takes it to mean "may everyone treat your name as holy," with God's name standing for His character and reputation. Guzik says the prayer puts God's name, kingdom and will before our own concerns. (Both URLs above.)

**v. 3**
- Guzik: "bread" means real, everyday food. He notes that early theologians allegorised it as Communion, as Christ, or as Scripture, and he quotes Calvin calling such readings "exceedingly absurd." It is bread for each day, not a stockpile. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-11/
- Constable: Luke's present tense and "each day" point to God's ongoing supply. The Greek word *epiousion* also carries the sense of "sufficient." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/luke-11.html

**v. 4**
- Constable: Luke says "sins" where Matthew uses the Jewish idiom "debts." Because believers are already forgiven, he reads this petition as forgiveness that keeps up fellowship with the Father. He reads "lead us not" as a figure of speech asking for help to stay faithful under testing. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/luke-11.html
- Guzik: "for we also forgive" takes for granted that forgiven people will forgive others. "Temptation" means a test, and he quotes France: God tempts no one but allows testing, so disciples should pray to be spared it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-11/ He also quotes Spurgeon's warning that praying "lead us not into temptation" while deliberately walking into sin is 'shameful profanity.' https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-11/

**vv. 5–7**
- Constable and Guzik: hospitality was a sacred duty. In a one-room house the whole family, and often the animals, slept together, so getting up at midnight would wake everyone. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/11-8.html; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-11/

**v. 8 (debated word)**
- The older reading is persistence. Matthew Henry: "We prevail with men by importunity because they are displeased with it, but with God because he is pleased with it." Barnes points out that the Latin Vulgate adds "if he shall continue knocking." Gill compares the parable of the widow in Luke 18. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/11-8.html
- The newer reading is shamelessness. Constable says the Greek word anaideia means shameless, or avoidance of shame, not persistence. On this view the sleeper gets up to avoid being shamed. Jesus is drawing a contrast with God, not a comparison. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/11-8.html Precept Austin also says the householder is not being LIKENED to God. Rather, they are being CONTRASTED to God. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-11-commentary
- Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel) says Jesus is teaching by contrast: with God you don't have to be persistent. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/11-8.html
- Guzik (Calvary Chapel, listed under Pentecostal/charismatic in your site list): persistence doesn't persuade a reluctant God; it changes us. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-11/
- Godbey (Wesleyan-Holiness) pushes the "shameless" idea furthest. He says you must reach the point of shamelessness for prayer to prevail. https://studylight.org/commentaries/ges/luke-11.html

**vv. 9–10**
- Guzik, quoting Morris: all three verbs describe continuing action, so the sense is "keep on asking." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-11/ Precept Austin adds that seeking is stronger than asking; knocking is stronger than seeking. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-11-commentary
- Guzik's devotional: God's answer isn't always "yes," but "no" and "not yet" also come from a loving God. https://enduringword.com/blog-archive/weekly-devotionals/knocking-on-heavens-door/
- Constable: the promise is to everyone who asks, not only to the persistent. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/luke-11.html

**vv. 11–12**
- Constable, citing Edersheim: a snake can look like a fish, and scorpions were sometimes thought to breed in eggs. Such a swap would be deceit and danger, not a gift. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/luke-11.html

**v. 13 (where traditions differ)**
- Gill notes that the Vulgate reads "good Spirit." He takes the verse to mean the gifts and graces of the Spirit. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/amp/luke/11-13.html
- Matthew Henry (Puritan): the gift of the Spirit is something every believer should earnestly and constantly pray for. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Luk/Luk_011.cfm
- Spurgeon (Baptist) compares Matthew 7:11 and concludes that the Holy Spirit stands for all "good things," which makes this a comprehensive prayer. https://biblehub.com/sermons/luke/11-13.htm
- Assemblies of God (Pentecostal): if you want the baptism in the Holy Spirit, ask Him to fill you, knowing He will give you His marvelous Holy Spirit according to Luke 11:13. https://news.ag.org/en/articles/news/2018/10/what%20every%20believer%20should%20know%20about%20receiving%20the%20baptism%20in%20the%20holy%20spirit
- Constable (dispensational evangelical) disagrees. When Jesus said this, the Spirit didn't yet live in every believer. Believers now don't need to ask for the Spirit, because He is given when they trust Christ (Rom 8:9). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/luke-11.html
- Godbey (Holiness) sees the Spirit working in stages: convicting sinners, regenerating penitents, and sanctifying consecrated believers. https://studylight.org/commentaries/ges/luke-11.html

**vv. 14–16**
- Constable: the healing was a sign of Jesus' messiahship. "Beelzebul" probably comes from *baal zebul*, "Prince Baal," or may mean "lord of the dwelling." Asking for a further sign was a provocation. He also notes that the opposition seen in the leaders is now showing up in the crowd. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/luke-11.html
- Precept Austin: the crowds treated Jesus as a spectacle, but not a Messiah to be believed in. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-11-commentary

**vv. 17–18**
- Guzik: if Jesus worked for Satan and against Satan at the same time, Satan's kingdom would be in civil war and couldn't stand. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-11/

**v. 19**
- Henry: "your sons" means Jewish exorcists, perhaps even Pharisees, whom nobody accused of working with Satan. To condemn in Jesus what they allowed in their own people was hypocrisy. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Luk/Luk_011.cfm Constable makes the same double-standard point and cites Acts 19:13–14. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/luke-11.html

**v. 20**
- Constable: "finger of God" echoes Exodus 8:19, where Pharaoh's magicians admitted God was at work. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/luke-11.html
- Guzik, following Pate: "if" here means "since." Jesus isn't expressing any doubt. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-11/

**vv. 21–22**
- Constable: Satan is the strong man and Jesus the stronger one. Satan's armour is his demons, and his plunder is the people he holds captive. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/luke-11.html
- Henry: every conversion is Christ's victory over the devil, and Christ shares the spoils with believers. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Luk/Luk_011.cfm
- Guzik: Christ plunders Satan's kingdom "one life at a time." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-11/

**v. 23**
- Constable: there is no neutral ground. The image switches from battle to harvest and flock: gathering versus scattering. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/luke-11.html
- Henry: those who rejected Christ's teaching and made light of His miracles were siding with the devil. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Luk/Luk_011.cfm

**vv. 24–26**
- J.C. Ryle (Anglican), quoted by Precept Austin: the words apply to the Jewish nation of Jesus' day, but the main lesson is for each of us: never to be satisfied with religious reformation without heart conversion. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-11-commentary
- Guzik: someone set free but not filled with Jesus ends up worse off. Christ came to fill the house, not just to empty it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-11/
- Constable, following Marshall: a warning to critics who cast out demons without offering the gospel, leaving people spiritually empty. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/luke-11.html

**v. 27 (with Jesus' reply in v. 28; Catholic and Protestant readings differ)**
- Older Protestant view: Barnes says Jesus agrees it was an honour to be His mother but calls obeying God's word a higher honour. Gill points to a similar Jewish blessing ("blessed is she that bore him") and says the words praise Christ more than Mary. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/11-27.htm
- Spurgeon (Baptist): Jesus said "Yes" first, then added a higher truth. Mary's blessedness lay mainly in her faith. https://ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons32/sermons32.xliv.html
- Piper (desiringgod.org): Scripture holds us back from the kind of exaltation of Mary that we find in the Roman Catholic Church. https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/how-to-become-the-mother-of-jesus
- MacArthur (gty.org) cites this passage against special veneration of Mary. He says Mary was blessed because she was obedient to the Word of God—the same as any other believer. https://gty.org/library/blog/B150327/the-seven-last-sayings-of-christ-a-provision-for-his-mother
- Constable: the passage should warn us against venerating Mary too highly. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/luke-11.html
- Catholic view (catholic.com): the Greek word *menoun* can mean "indeed, much more." Drawing on John Paul II's *Redemptoris Mater*, the article says Jesus is giving Mary a twofold blessing, as mother by nature and in faith, not denying she is blessed. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/that-time-jesus-dissed-his-mom A second catholic.com article says her blessedness isn't because of bloodlines but because of faith (Luke 1:45). https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/jesus-puts-mary-in-her-place
